source.title: Scalable Autoregressive Monocular Depth Estimation
source.authors: Jin-Hong Wang; Jian Liu; Dongqi Tang; Wei-Qiang Wang; Wen-Tong Li; D. Chen; Jin-Tai Chen; Jian Wu

record.tranche_reason: The study evaluates model scaling for monocular depth estimation, an image-vision setting, and reports performance across model sizes. It does not reproduce language-model held-out cross-entropy scaling.
record.gate_note: The study reports DAR performance at multiple parameter counts, which bears on scaling in another modality. It does not fit or test a power-law curve. The cited language-model scaling-law results are background, not findings from this study. Table 4 is a zero-shot dataset comparison without a size sweep; Table 5 mainly reports component ablations rather than an isolated scaling-law test.
record.test_reason: The paper cites Kaplan and Hoffmann to motivate scaling its own depth model. It reports its method's RMSE at three sizes (440M, 1B, 2B), with data and epochs fixed and the ViT-L encoder shared. It fits no power law, reports no loss-vs-scale form or exponent, and has no compute or data axis. Monotone task-metric gains over three points cannot show a power-law form, so no version is tested. The 'scaling laws akin to LLMs' statement is asserted, not measured.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. The authors conclude DAR is an effective, scalable autoregressive depth estimator that sets SOTA on KITTI and NYU and generalizes zero-shot. The 'scaling laws akin to LLMs' remark appears in the introduction and rests only on three model sizes, with no fitted law.
record.recipe_differences: The study scales vision models for monocular depth estimation and reports depth RMSE, rather than scaling language models against held-out cross-entropy or testing compute-optimal allocations. It reports performance at three sizes but no power-law fit.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported performance values are for two different datasets, NYU Depth v2 and KITTI; the study reports separate results for each.

fits_no_version.finding: Depth RMSE falls monotonically but modestly as the DAR model grows from 440M to 2.0B (about 4.5x) with data fixed. NYU RMSE goes 0.217 to 0.214 to 0.205 (about 5.5%). KITTI RMSE goes 1.839 to 1.823 to 1.799 (about 2%).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In supervised monocular depth estimation, increasing autoregressive decoder size improves task error monotonically over 440M–2B parameters; no power-law form is established.

record.problems: The scaling evidence consists of three model sizes and reported task metrics; no power-law fitting, uncertainty estimates, or compute-optimal allocation analysis is reported.
record.rows_left_out: Table 5 component-ablation values are not included because the comparisons change model components as well as size and are not an isolated size-scaling series. Table 4 reports zero-shot dataset performance but no size sweep.

untested.parts: Language-model pretraining loss vs parameters, tokens or compute.
Extrapolation from small-run fits to larger runs.
Shape at fixed parameter count; depth and width change together with size in Table 1.
Power-law form in vision or depth estimation. Only three sizes are reported, with no fit, no data or compute axis, and a task metric rather than loss.
Downstream predictability from scale or loss.
Dependence of fits on setup or fitting choices.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's V5 limits_scope label is removed: three task-metric points with no fit cannot test power-law form. Table 1 scales layers, hidden size and heads together. The shared ViT-L encoder is constant, and it is unclear whether the stated model size includes it. Training is fixed at 25 epochs on single datasets. No uncertainty is reported.

versions.untested_parts: Language-model held-out pretraining cross-entropy scaling with parameters, tokens, or compute.
Whether power laws fitted on small runs predict much larger runs.
Compute-optimal parameter/token allocations and their relationship to compute.
Controlled comparisons of depth, width, or other architecture choices at fixed parameter count.

The study evaluates one visual task, monocular depth estimation, but does not fit a power-law form or estimate exponents. It does not test other modalities or regimes such as repeated data, fine-tuning, or transfer.
Downstream language-model task performance as a function of scale or pretraining loss.
Dependence of fitted exponents or compute-optimal splits on fitting choices or setup, and departures from a single power law.
